claim: In amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS), spinal motor neurons (SpMN) progressively degenerate while a subset of cranial motor neurons (CrMN) are spared until late stages of the disease.
source: In amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS) spinal motor neurons (SpMN) progressively degenerate while a subset of cranial motor neurons (CrMN) are spared until late stages of the disease.
evidence: This is a well-established clinical observation about ALS pathology cited in the introduction with references to Gizzi et al., 1992; Okamoto et al., 1993; Lawyer and Netsky, 1953; Kanning et al., 2010.

claim: ESC-derived CrMNs accumulate less human (h)SOD1 than SpMNs over time.
source: ESC-derived CrMNs accumulate less human (h)SOD1 and insoluble p62 than SpMNs over time.
evidence: This claim is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 3 comparing hSOD1 accumulation between iCrMNs and iSpMNs at Day 2 and Day 15.

claim: ESC-derived CrMNs accumulate less insoluble p62 than SpMNs over time.
source: ESC-derived CrMNs accumulate less human (h)SOD1 and insoluble p62 than SpMNs over time.
evidence: This claim is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 6B-C comparing p62 accumulation between Day 15 iCrMNs and iSpMNs.

claim: ESC-derived CrMNs have higher proteasome activity to degrade misfolded proteins than SpMNs.
source: ESC-derived CrMNs have higher proteasome activity to degrade misfolded proteins and are intrinsically more resistant to chemically-induced proteostatic stress than SpMNs.
evidence: This claim is supported by proteasome activity measurements shown in Figure 9C and mass spectrometry data in Figure 9B showing higher levels of 20S core subunits in iCrMNs.

claim: ESC-derived CrMNs are intrinsically more resistant to chemically-induced proteostatic stress than SpMNs.
source: ESC-derived CrMNs have higher proteasome activity to degrade misfolded proteins and are intrinsically more resistant to chemically-induced proteostatic stress than SpMNs.
evidence: This claim is supported by survival assay data shown in Figure 7B-D demonstrating differential survival of iCrMNs and iSpMNs to tunicamycin, CPA, and thapsigargin treatment.

claim: Chemical activation of the proteasome rescues SpMN sensitivity to proteostatic stress.
source: Chemical and genetic activation of the proteasome rescues SpMN sensitivity to proteostatic stress.
evidence: This claim is supported by survival data in Figure 10D showing that PD169316 treatment improved iSpMN survival to CPA-induced stress.

claim: Genetic activation of the proteasome rescues SpMN sensitivity to proteostatic stress.
source: Chemical and genetic activation of the proteasome rescues SpMN sensitivity to proteostatic stress.
evidence: This claim is supported by survival data in Figure 10F showing that PSMB5 overexpression improved iSpMN survival to CPA treatment.

claim: In the hSOD1 G93A mouse model, ALS-resistant CrMNs accumulate less insoluble hSOD1 than SpMNs.
source: In agreement, the hSOD1 G93A mouse model reveals that ALS-resistant CrMNs accumulate less insoluble hSOD1 and p62-containing inclusions than SpMNs.
evidence: This claim is supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 1A-B demonstrating that 34% of SpMNs contain hSOD1 aggregates while 0% of O/TrMNs contain aggregates in P100 SOD1 G93A mice.

claim: In the hSOD1 G93A mouse model, ALS-resistant CrMNs accumulate fewer p62-containing inclusions than SpMNs.
source: In agreement, the hSOD1 G93A mouse model reveals that ALS-resistant CrMNs accumulate less insoluble hSOD1 and p62-containing inclusions than SpMNs.
evidence: This claim is supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 6D-E demonstrating that over 40% of lumbar SpMNs accumulated p62 positive inclusions while 0% of oculomotor neurons had p62 aggregates.

claim: Primary-derived ALS-resistant CrMNs are more resistant than SpMNs to proteostatic stress.
source: Primary-derived ALS-resistant CrMNs are also more resistant than SpMNs to proteostatic stress.
evidence: This claim is supported by survival assay data shown in Figure 8B-C demonstrating that primary O/TrMNs were more resistant than primary SpMNs to tunicamycin and CPA treatment.

claim: Oculomotor, trochlear and abducens motor neurons are typically spared in ALS, allowing patients to retain eye movement until late stages of the disease.
source: While most spinal motor neurons (SpMNs) degenerate during ALS progression, a subset of cranial motor neurons (CrMNs: oculomotor, trochlear and abducens motor neurons) are typically spared, allowing patients to retain eye movement until late stages of the disease (Gizzi et al., 1992; Okamoto et al., 1993; Lawyer and Netsky, 1953; Kanning et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to clinical observations in ALS patients.

claim: Oculomotor and trochlear motor neurons are more resistant than SpMNs to neurodegeneration in the ALS mouse model expressing human (h) SOD1 G93A.
source: Oculomotor and trochlear motor neurons are also more resistant than SpMNs to neurodegeneration in the ALS mouse model expressing human (h) SOD1 G93A (Haenggeli and Kato, 2002).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Haenggeli and Kato, 2002.

claim: Approximately 90% of ALS patients suffer from sporadic ALS while approximately 10% of ALS cases are familial.
source: With shared clinical manifestations, ~90% of patients suffer from sporadic ALS while ~10% of ALS cases are familial.
evidence: This is a well-established epidemiological fact about ALS.

claim: More than fifty genes involved in different biological processes have been reported to contribute to familial ALS cases.
source: More than fifty genes involved in different biological processes have been reported to contribute to the familial ALS cases. (Rosen, 1993; Taylor et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Rosen, 1993 and Taylor et al., 2016.

claim: One common hallmark found in both familial and sporadic ALS is the accumulation of aggregated proteins.
source: One common hallmark found in both familial and sporadic ALS is the accumulation of aggregated proteins, which is also shared by many other neurodegenerative diseases (Yerbury et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Yerbury et al., 2016.

claim: ALS mutations in SOD1, TARDBP, FUS and C9ORF72 generate proteins with a propensity to misfold and aggregate.
source: ALS mutations in SOD1, TARDBP (TAR DNA-binding protein 43 kDa), FUS (Fused in Sarcoma) and C9ORF72 generate proteins with a propensity to misfold and aggregate (Bruijn et al., 1998; Neumann et al., 2006; Deng et al., 2010; Zu et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to multiple studies on ALS-causing mutations.

claim: In both ALS patients and mouse models, SpMNs and astrocytes typically contain inclusions positive for ubiquitinated proteins and the ubiquitin-binding protein SQSTM1 (p62).
source: In both ALS patients and mouse models, SpMNs and astrocytes typically contain inclusions positive for ubiquitinated proteins and the ubiquitin-binding protein SQSTM1 (Sequestosome 1, also known as p62) (Leigh et al., 1991; Watanabe et al., 2001; Mizuno et al., 2006; Neumann et al., 2006; Gal et al., 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to multiple studies documenting protein inclusions in ALS.

claim: Soluble and misfolded proteins are degraded primarily by the ubiquitin proteasome system.
source: Soluble and misfolded proteins are degraded primarily by the ubiquitin proteasome system, while large protein aggregates are recognized and removed by the autophagy lysosome pathway (Dikic, 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Dikic, 2017 and represents established knowledge about protein degradation pathways.

claim: Large protein aggregates are recognized and removed by the autophagy lysosome pathway.
source: Soluble and misfolded proteins are degraded primarily by the ubiquitin proteasome system, while large protein aggregates are recognized and removed by the autophagy lysosome pathway (Dikic, 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Dikic, 2017 and represents established knowledge about protein degradation pathways.

claim: ALS-causing misfolding proteins, like mutant SOD1, can be degraded by both the proteasome and autophagy pathways.
source: Therefore, ALS-causing misfolding proteins, like mutant SOD1, can be degraded by both the proteasome and autophagy pathways (Kabuta et al., 2006; Castillo et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Kabuta et al., 2006 and Castillo et al., 2013.

claim: Mutations in genes encoding important components of degradation pathways can cause ALS, including UBQLN2, SQSTM1 (p62), OPTN, VCP, VAPB and TBK1.
source: Moreover, mutations in genes encoding important components of these degradation pathways can cause ALS (Taylor et al., 2016; Ghasemi and Brown, 2018), including UBQLN2 (Deng et al., 2011), SQSTM1 (p62) (Fecto et al., 2011; Rubino et al., 2012; Hirano et al., 2013), OPTN (Maruyama et al., 2010), VCP (Johnson et al., 2010), VAPB (Nishimura et al., 2004) and TBK1 (Freischmidt et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to multiple studies identifying ALS-causing mutations in degradation pathway genes.

claim: Matrix metallopeptidase 9 (MMP-9) is expressed only in the fast-fatigable α-motor neurons, a selective subtype of SpMNs vulnerable in ALS.
source: Matrix metallopeptidase 9 (MMP-9) is expressed only in the fast-fatigable α-motor neurons, a selective subtype of SpMNs vulnerable in ALS.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Kaplan et al., 2014 in the context of discussing differential motor neuron sensitivity.

claim: Reduction of MMP-9 significantly delayed muscle denervation of fast-fatigable α-motor neurons in the ALS mouse model expressing hSOD1 G93A.
source: Reduction of MMP-9 significantly delayed muscle denervation of fast-fatigable α-motor neurons in the ALS mouse model expressing hSOD1 G93A (Kaplan et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Kaplan et al., 2014.

claim: Expression of IGF-2 (insulin-like growth factor 2) is upregulated in the resistant oculomotor neurons.
source: Conversely, expression of IGF-2 (insulin-like growth factor 2) is upregulated in the resistant oculomotor neurons.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Allodi et al., 2016 in the context of discussing mechanisms of motor neuron resistance.

claim: Viral delivery of IGF-2 to the muscles of hSOD1 G93A mice extended life-span by 10%.
source: Viral delivery of IGF-2 to the muscles of hSOD1 G93A mice extended life-span by 10% (Allodi et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Allodi et al., 2016.

claim: During embryonic differentiation, Isl1 and Lhx3 transcription factors specify SpMN identity.
source: During embryonic differentiation, Isl1 and Lhx3 transcription factors specify SpMN identity (Thaler et al., 2002), while Isl1 and Phox2a are essential for CrMN differentiation (Morin et al., 1997; Hirsch et al., 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Thaler et al., 2002.

claim: Isl1 and Phox2a are essential for CrMN differentiation.
source: During embryonic differentiation, Isl1 and Lhx3 transcription factors specify SpMN identity (Thaler et al., 2002), while Isl1 and Phox2a are essential for CrMN differentiation (Morin et al., 1997; Hirsch et al., 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Morin et al., 1997 and Hirsch et al., 2007.

claim: A third of all SpMNs (34 ± 4.2%) contain aggregates of misfolded hSOD1 in postnatal day 100 SOD1 G93A mice.
source: Interestingly, we found that a third of all SpMNs (34 ± 4.2% [mean ± SEM]; 195 motor neurons from three mice) contain aggregates of misfolded hSOD1 while, by contrast, we were unable to detect any aggregation within O/TrMNs (328 motor neurons from three mice) (Figure 1A and B).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative immunostaining data from P100 SOD1 G93A mice shown in Figure 1A-B.

claim: No aggregation of misfolded hSOD1 was detected within O/TrMNs in postnatal day 100 SOD1 G93A mice.
source: Interestingly, we found that a third of all SpMNs (34 ± 4.2% [mean ± SEM]; 195 motor neurons from three mice) contain aggregates of misfolded hSOD1 while, by contrast, we were unable to detect any aggregation within O/TrMNs (328 motor neurons from three mice) (Figure 1A and B).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative immunostaining data from P100 SOD1 G93A mice shown in Figure 1A-B.

claim: O/TrMNs exhibited strikingly lower overall levels of misfolded hSOD1 compared to SpMNs, necessitating imaging under 5–10 times higher confocal laser intensity.
source: Additionally, O/TrMNs exhibited strikingly lower overall levels of misfolded hSOD1 compared to SpMNs, necessitating imaging under 5–10 times higher confocal laser intensity.
evidence: This claim is supported by imaging data shown in Figure 1A and Figure 1—figure supplement 1A.

claim: By Day 5, 87% of iCrMNs and 74% of iSpMNs survived compared to Day 2.
source: By Day 5, 87% of iCrMNs and 74% of iSpMNs survived compared to Day 2 (Figure 1G).
evidence: This claim is supported by survival assay data shown in Figure 1G.

claim: By Day 25, 52% of iCrMNs and 31% of iSpMNs survived.
source: By Day 25, 52% of iCrMNs and 31% of iSpMNs survived.
evidence: This claim is supported by survival assay data shown in Figure 1G.

claim: 88% of primary O/TrMNs and 72% of primary SpMNs survived on DIV 7.
source: With the optimized supplement cocktail [10 ng/mL GDNF, 10 ng/mL BDNF, 10 ng/mL CNTF, 100 μM 3-isobutyl-1-methylxanthine (IBMX) and 10 μM Forskolin], 88% of primary O/TrMNs and 72% of primary SpMNs survived on DIV 7 (Figure 1D).
evidence: This claim is supported by survival assay data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: On DIV 14, 71% of primary O/TrMNs and only 42% of primary SpMNs survived.
source: On DIV 14, 71% of primary O/TrMNs and only 42% of primary SpMNs survived.
evidence: This claim is supported by survival assay data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: iSpMNs accumulated over two times more soluble hSOD1 A4V and G93A by Day 15 compared to Day 2.
source: While iCrMNs maintained similar levels of soluble hSOD1 mutant proteins from Day two to Day 15, iSpMNs accumulated over two times more soluble hSOD1 A4V and G93A by Day 15 compared to Day 2 (Figure 3B,C).
evidence: This claim is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 3B-C.

claim: iSpMNs accumulated approximately 3 times more insoluble hSOD1 A4V and G93A than iCrMNs on Day 15.
source: Moreover, iSpMNs also accumulated ~3 times more insoluble hSOD1 A4V and G93A than iCrMNs on Day 15 (Figure 3B,D).
evidence: This claim is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 3B,D.

claim: 100 nM of MG-132 reduced proteasome activity by approximately 30% in both iCrMNs and iSpMNs.
source: 100 nM of MG-132 reduced proteasome activity by ~30% in both iCrMNs (68.27 ± 10.30% compared to DMSO) and iSpMNs (67.63 ± 9.49% compared to DMSO, iCrMNs versus iSpMNs p=0.47 by Student's t-test, n = 3).
evidence: This claim is supported by proteasome activity measurements using Suc-LLVY-AMC hydrolysis assay.

claim: iSpMNs accumulated approximately 2 fold more insoluble mutant hSOD1 when the proteasome was compromised by MG-132.
source: iSpMNs accumulated ~2 fold more insoluble mutant hSOD1 when the proteasome was compromised (1.73 ± 0.21 fold more hSOD1 A4V, p=0.03; 1.93 ± 0.23 fold more hSOD1 G93A, p=0.02) (Figure 4C), suggesting that proteins that would have normally been degraded by the proteasome instead contributed to the insoluble aggregates.
evidence: This claim is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 4B-C comparing MG-132 and DMSO treated neurons.

claim: iCrMNs accumulated approximately 8.5 fold more insoluble hSOD1 A4V and approximately 5.3 fold more insoluble hSOD1 G93A compared to DMSO control after MG-132 treatment.
source: Revealingly, iCrMNs accumulated ~8.5 fold more insoluble hSOD1 A4V and ~5.3 fold more insoluble hSOD1 G93A compared to DMSO control (Figure 4B,C).
evidence: This claim is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 4B-C.

claim: MG-132 treatment resulted in accumulation of more soluble and insoluble p62 proteins in both iCrMNs and iSpMNs, with iSpMNs and iCrMNs accumulating 2–3 fold and 6–10 fold more insoluble p62 protein respectively.
source: The mild reduction of proteasome activity resulted in accumulation of more soluble and insoluble p62 proteins in both iCrMNs and iSpMNs, with iSpMNs and iCrMNs accumulating 2–3 fold and 6–10 fold more insoluble p62 protein respectively (Figure 5D,E).
evidence: This claim is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 5D-E.

claim: Over 40% of lumbar SpMNs accumulated p62 positive inclusions in hSOD1 G93A mice at postnatal days 66 and 97.
source: While over 40% of lumbar SpMNs accumulated p62 positive inclusions, there were no oculomotor neurons with protein aggregates containing p62 (Figure 6D,E).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 6D-E from hSOD1 G93A mice.

claim: There were no oculomotor neurons with protein aggregates containing p62 in hSOD1 G93A mice at postnatal days 66 and 97.
source: While over 40% of lumbar SpMNs accumulated p62 positive inclusions, there were no oculomotor neurons with protein aggregates containing p62 (Figure 6D,E).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 6D-E from hSOD1 G93A mice.

claim: More iSpMNs (approximately 15%) exhibited p62-positive cytoplasmic aggregates than did iCrMNs (approximately 5%) on Day 5.
source: Consistent with in vivo observations, more iSpMNs (~15%) exhibited p62-positive cytoplasmic aggregates than did iCrMNs (~5%) (Figure 6F).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunocytochemistry data shown in Figure 6F.

claim: Inhibition of the proteasome by MG-132 treatment resulted in nearly 50% of iCrMNs containing p62 aggregates, compared to approximately 30% of iSpMNs.
source: Interestingly, inhibition of the proteasome by MG-132 treatment had a greater effect on iCrMNs, nearly 50% of which contained p62 aggregates, compared to ~30% of iSpMNs (Figure 6F).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunocytochemistry data shown in Figure 6F.

claim: 150 ng/ml tunicamycin was significantly more toxic to iSpMNs than to iCrMNs (65 ± 6% survival for iCrMNs and 47 ± 3% for iSpMNs).
source: While 100 ng/ml tunicamycin affected both cell types nearly equally (88 ± 4% survival for iCrMNs and 83 ± 5% for iSpMNs, respectively), 150 ng/ml tunicamycin was significantly more toxic to iSpMNs than to iCrMNs (65 ± 6% survival for iCrMNs and 47 ± 3% for iSpMNs, respectively) (Figure 7B).
evidence: This claim is supported by survival assay data shown in Figure 7B.

claim: At 300 ng/mL tunicamycin, close to 50% (49% ± 5%) of iCrMNs survived compared to only about 10% (11% ± 1%) of iSpMNs.
source: iCrMNs were consistently more resistant to tunicamycin up through the highest concentration tested (300 ng/mL), at which close to 50% (49% ± 5%) of iCrMNs survived compared to only about 10% (11% ± 1%) of iSpMNs.
evidence: This claim is supported by survival assay data shown in Figure 7B.

claim: 10 μM CPA treatment resulted in iCrMNs displaying an insensitivity to treatment (103 ± 6%) compared to only approximately 80% (75% ± 4%) of iSpMNs surviving.
source: 10 μM CPA, however, was sufficient to reveal a survival difference, with iCrMNs displaying an insensitivity to treatment (103 ± 6%) compared to only ~80% (75% ± 4%) of iSpMNs surviving (Figure 7C).
evidence: This claim is supported by survival assay data shown in Figure 7C.

claim: At 40 μM CPA, the survival of iSpMNs was only about 10% (9% ± 1%) compared to nearly 40% (37% ± 3%) of iCrMNs.
source: This differential survival trend was maintained through the highest concentration tested (40 μM), at which the survival of iSpMNs was only about 10% (9% ± 1%) compared to nearly 40% (37% ± 3%) of iCrMNs.
evidence: This claim is supported by survival assay data shown in Figure 7C.

claim: iSpMNs showed higher induction of sXBP1, GRP78 and ATF4 than iCrMNs after CPA treatment.
source: iSpMNs showed higher induction of sXBP1, GRP78 and ATF4 than iCrMNs (Figure 7—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1 measuring UPR markers after CPA treatment.

claim: Brefeldin A was equally toxic to both iCrMNs and iSpMNs.
source: Brefeldin A was equally toxic to both cell types (Figure 7E).
evidence: This claim is supported by survival assay data shown in Figure 7E.

claim: Primary O/TrMNs were significantly more resistant than primary SpMNs to tunicamycin treatment within 100–250 ng/ml.
source: Primary O/TrMNs were significantly more resistant than primary SpMNs to tunicamycin treatment within 100–250 ng/ml and to CPA treatment within 10–25 µM (Figure 8B–C).
evidence: This claim is supported by survival assay data shown in Figure 8B.

claim: Primary O/TrMNs were significantly more resistant than primary SpMNs to CPA treatment within 10–25 µM.
source: Primary O/TrMNs were significantly more resistant than primary SpMNs to tunicamycin treatment within 100–250 ng/ml and to CPA treatment within 10–25 µM (Figure 8B–C).
evidence: This claim is supported by survival assay data shown in Figure 8C.

claim: iCrMNs contain higher levels of all 20S core subunits of the proteasome than iSpMNs.
source: Among the differences, we noted that iCrMNs contain higher levels of all 20S core subunits of the proteasome than iSpMNs (Figure 9B).
evidence: This claim is supported by unbiased mass spectrometry data shown in Figure 9B.

claim: Differences in proteasome subunit levels are not found among regulatory subunits of the proteasome.
source: Interestingly, these differences are not found among regulatory subunits of the proteasome (Figure 9B).
evidence: This claim is supported by mass spectrometry data shown in Figure 9B.

claim: Non-transgenic iCrMNs had a higher proteasome activity than iSpMNs at Day 2 and 5 in culture.
source: Non-transgenic iCrMNs had a higher proteasome activity than iSpMNs at Day 2 and 5 in culture (Figure 9C).
evidence: This claim is supported by proteasome activity measurements shown in Figure 9C.

claim: PD169316 treatment increased chymotrypsin-like activity of the 20S proteasome in iSpMNs and iCrMNs in a dosage dependent manner.
source: In agreement to what has been described in other neuronal cell types, PD169316 treatment increased chymotrypsin-like activity of the 20S proteasome in iSpMNs and iCrMNs in a dosage dependent manner (Figure 10B).
evidence: This claim is supported by proteasome activity measurements shown in Figure 10B.

claim: 0.25–2 μM PD169316 did not affect the survival of iCrMNs or iSpMNs in culture.
source: 0.25–2 μM PD169316 did not affect the survival of iCrMNs or iSpMNs in culture (Figure 10C).
evidence: This claim is supported by survival assay data shown in Figure 10C.

claim: Co-treatment of PD169316 improved the survival of iSpMNs from 66 ± 4% with no PD169316 to 80 ± 4% with 2 µM PD169316 in the presence of 10 µM CPA.
source: In a concentration dependent manner, co-treatment of PD169316 improved the survival of iSpMNs from 66 ± 4% with no PD169316% to 80 ± 4% with 2 µM PD169316 (Figure 10D).
evidence: This claim is supported by survival assay data shown in Figure 10D.

claim: 0–2 μM PD169316 treatment did not significantly enhance iCrMN survival to 10 µM CPA.
source: 0–2 μM PD169316 treatment did not significantly enhance iCrMN survival to 10 µM CPA (Figure 10D).
evidence: This claim is supported by survival assay data shown in Figure 10D.

claim: Enhancing proteasome activity by 2 µM PD169316 was sufficient to increase iSpMN survival to phenocopy the basal iCrMN resistance to 10 µM CPA treatment.
source: Notably, enhancing proteasome activity by 2 µM PD169316 was sufficient to increase iSpMN survival to phenocopy the basal iCrMN resistance to 10 µM CPA treatment (indicated by the red dash line in Figure 10D).
evidence: This claim is supported by survival assay data shown in Figure 10D.

claim: PSMB5 expression significantly improved iSpMN survival to CPA treatment compared to LacZ infected controls.
source: These experiments revealed that PSMB5 expression significantly improved iSpMN survival to CPA treatment compared to LacZ infected controls but showed no effects in iCrMNs (Figure 10F).
evidence: This claim is supported by survival assay data shown in Figure 10F using lentiviral expression of PSMB5.

claim: PSMB5 expression showed no effects on iCrMN survival to CPA treatment.
source: These experiments revealed that PSMB5 expression significantly improved iSpMN survival to CPA treatment compared to LacZ infected controls but showed no effects in iCrMNs (Figure 10F).
evidence: This claim is supported by survival assay data shown in Figure 10F.

claim: CPA treatment significantly increased the accumulation of insoluble hSOD1 A4V.
source: CPA treatment significantly increased the accumulation of insoluble hSOD1 A4V (Figure 7—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: This claim is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 2A-B.

claim: iCrMNs accumulated less insoluble hSOD1 A4V than iSpMNs regardless of DMSO or CPA treatment.
source: iCrMNs accumulated less insoluble hSOD1 A4V than iSpMNs regardless of the treatment (Figure 7—figure supplement 2C).
evidence: This claim is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 2C.

claim: The hSOD1 A4V and hSOD1 G93A transgenes were expressed at similar levels between iCrMNs and iSpMNs on Day 7.
source: The differential accumulation of hSOD1 proteins between iCrMNs and iSpMNs was not secondary to cell-specific silencing or upregulation of the transgene as both the hSOD1 A4V and hSOD1 G93A transgenes were expressed at similar levels between iCrMNs and iSpMNs on Day 7, measured by RT-qPCR.
evidence: This claim is supported by RT-qPCR measurements showing no significant difference in hSOD1 mRNA levels between iCrMNs and iSpMNs.

claim: The translation efficiency of hSOD1 was similar between iCrMNs and iSpMNs as measured by polysome profiling.
source: The translation efficiency of hSOD1 was also similar between iCrMNs and iSpMNs as measured by polysome profiling (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by polysome profiling data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: iCrMNs have a cell-autonomous mechanism to restrain the accumulation of hSOD1 mutant proteins.
source: Therefore, it is likely that iCrMNs have a cell-autonomous mechanism to restrain the accumulation of hSOD1 mutant proteins, and perhaps other misfolded proteins.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the observation that hSOD1 mRNA and translation are similar between iCrMNs and iSpMNs, yet protein accumulation differs.

claim: A substantial fraction of mutant hSOD1 protein is being targeted for degradation by the proteasome in iCrMNs.
source: Thus, a substantial fraction of mutant hSOD1 protein is being targeted for degradation by the proteasome in iCrMNs.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the observation that MG-132 treatment caused much greater accumulation of insoluble hSOD1 in iCrMNs than iSpMNs.

claim: iCrMNs may rely on the proteasome to a greater extent than iSpMNs to degrade mutant misfolded hSOD1 proteins and reduce their accumulation in insoluble aggregates.
source: These results imply that iCrMNs may rely on the proteasome to a greater extent than iSpMNs to degrade mutant misfolded hSOD1 proteins and reduce their accumulation in insoluble aggregates.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the differential response to MG-132 treatment between iCrMNs and iSpMNs.

claim: There is an intrinsic difference between iCrMNs and iSpMNs in their use of the ubiquitin proteasome system to degrade misfolded proteins that would otherwise contribute to insoluble protein aggregates.
source: Therefore, we conclude that there is an intrinsic difference between iCrMNs and iSpMNs in their use of the ubiquitin proteasome system to degrade misfolded proteins that would otherwise contribute to insoluble protein aggregates.
evidence: This claim is supported by the differential accumulation of ubiquitinated proteins and p62 after MG-132 treatment shown in Figure 5.

claim: iSpMNs experienced a stronger level of proteostatic stress than iCrMNs to the same CPA treatment.
source: This suggests that iSpMNs experienced a stronger level of proteostatic stress than iCrMNs to the same CPA treatment, presumably because they are less efficient than iCrMNs at degrading misfolded proteins.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the higher induction of UPR markers in iSpMNs compared to iCrMNs after CPA treatment.

claim: Additional proteostatic stress accelerates the accumulation of insoluble hSOD1 mutant proteins.
source: These results suggest that additional proteostatic stress accelerates the accumulation of insoluble hSOD1 mutant proteins and that iCrMNs maintain a superior capability to deal with misfolded proteins under CPA treatment.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the observation that CPA treatment increased insoluble hSOD1 A4V accumulation.

claim: iCrMNs maintain a superior capability to deal with misfolded proteins under CPA treatment.
source: These results suggest that additional proteostatic stress accelerates the accumulation of insoluble hSOD1 mutant proteins and that iCrMNs maintain a superior capability to deal with misfolded proteins under CPA treatment.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the observation that iCrMNs accumulated less insoluble hSOD1 A4V than iSpMNs under both DMSO and CPA treatment.

claim: Culture conditions do not favor iCrMNs' ability to resist all chemical stress.
source: The comparable sensitivities of iCrMNs and iSpMNs to brefeldin A suggest that culture conditions do not favor iCrMNs' ability to resist all chemical stress.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the observation that brefeldin A was equally toxic to both iCrMNs and iSpMNs.

claim: ALS-resistant neuronal fate is associated with an intrinsically superior capacity to deal with generalized proteostatic stress.
source: To test if ALS-resistant neuronal fate is associated with an intrinsically superior capacity to deal with generalized proteostatic stress, we compared the sensitivity of non-transgenic mouse primary ALS-resistant O/TrMNs and ALS-sensitive SpMNs to tunicamycin and CPA.
evidence: This claim is supported by the observation that primary O/TrMNs were more resistant than primary SpMNs to proteostatic stress, confirming predictions from ESC-derived neurons.

claim: The upregulation of core proteasome proteins in iCrMNs is due to post-transcriptional mechanisms.
source: Of note, RNA-seq experiments did not reveal this difference, which seems to be due to post-transcriptional mechanisms.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the observation that proteomic data showed differences in proteasome subunit levels while RNA-seq did not.

claim: iCrMNs have a higher capacity to degrade misfolding proteins and prevent the accumulation of insoluble aggregates because they have a higher proteasome activity than iSpMNs.
source: Together, these results suggest that iCrMN have a higher capacity to degrade misfolding proteins and prevent the accumulation of insoluble aggregates because they have a higher proteasome activity than iSpMNs.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the combination of proteomic data showing higher 20S core subunit levels and functional data showing higher proteasome activity in iCrMNs.

claim: A superior proteostatic capacity could be an intrinsic and disease relevant mechanism underlying CrMN resistance to ALS.
source: This superior proteostatic capacity could be an intrinsic and disease relevant mechanism underlying CrMN resistance to ALS.
evidence: This claim is supported by the convergence of in vitro ESC-derived neuron data, primary neuron data, and in vivo mouse model data.

claim: ESC-derived iCrMNs and iSpMNs recapitulated the differential accumulation of insoluble hSOD1 observed in vivo.
source: By over-expressing hSOD1 mutant proteins, ESC-derived induced CrMNs (iCrMNs) and SpMNs (iSpMNs) recapitulated the differential accumulation of insoluble hSOD1 in vitro and revealed more efficient proteasomal degradation of misfolded proteins in iCrMNs than SpMNs.
evidence: This claim is supported by western blot data comparing hSOD1 accumulation in iCrMNs and iSpMNs shown in Figure 3.

claim: ESC-derived neurons revealed more efficient proteasomal degradation of misfolded proteins in iCrMNs than SpMNs.
source: By over-expressing hSOD1 mutant proteins, ESC-derived induced CrMNs (iCrMNs) and SpMNs (iSpMNs) recapitulated the differential accumulation of insoluble hSOD1 in vitro and revealed more efficient proteasomal degradation of misfolded proteins in iCrMNs than SpMNs.
evidence: This claim is supported by MG-132 treatment experiments shown in Figures 4 and 5.

claim: The ESC-based platform has predictive value for identifying cell-autonomous properties that contribute to cell specific differential vulnerability to ALS.
source: Combining the results from hSOD1 G93A mice and primary motor neuron cultures, these data confirm our hypothesis generated from ESC-derived motor neurons that ALS-resistant CrMNs are more resistant to proteostatic stress than SpMNs. It also highlights the predictive value of this ESC-based in vitro platform for the study of cell-autonomous properties that contribute to the cell specific differential vulnerability to ALS.
evidence: This claim is supported by the concordance between ESC-derived neuron findings and in vivo/primary neuron validation.

claim: CrMNs take better advantage of the ubiquitin proteasome system to degrade misfolded proteins and maintain proteostasis.
source: Therefore, our comparative study of ESC-derived iCrMNs and iSpMNs identified that CrMNs take better advantage of the ubiquitin proteasome system to degrade misfolded proteins and maintain proteostasis.
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple lines of evidence including MG-132 experiments, proteasome activity measurements, and proteomic analysis.

claim: Persistent activation of p38 was observed in motor neurons beginning in the presymptomatic stages of the disease in hSOD1 G93A mice.
source: In hSOD1 G93A mice, persistent activation of p38 was observed in motor neurons beginning in the presymptomatic stages of the disease (Tortarolo et al., 2003; Holasek et al., 2005; Morfini et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Tortarolo et al., 2003; Holasek et al., 2005; Morfini et al., 2013.

claim: Chemical inhibition of p38 enhanced SpMN survival and rescued axonal transport defects.
source: Chemical inhibition of p38 enhanced SpMN survival and rescued axonal transport defects (Dewil et al., 2007; Gibbs et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Dewil et al., 2007 and Gibbs et al., 2018.

claim: The protective effects of p38 inhibitor treatment may benefit from enhanced activity of the proteasome and thereby improved proteostasis of misfolded proteins.
source: Our data now suggest that these protective effects, via the treatment of p38 inhibitors, may also benefit from enhanced activity of the proteasome and thereby improved proteostasis of misfolded proteins.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the observation that PD169316, a p38 inhibitor, enhanced proteasome activity and improved iSpMN survival.

claim: PSMB5 overexpression upregulates and increases the activity of all three catalytic β subunits and leads to integration of free α subunits into de novo assembled proteasomes.
source: PSMB5 overexpression had been shown to upregulate and increase the activity of all three catalytic β subunits and lead to integration of free α subunits into de novo assembled proteasomes, increasing proteasome activity and fibroblast survival to oxidative stress (Chondrogianni et al., 2005).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Chondrogianni et al., 2005.

claim: Over-expression of mutant hSOD1 induces ALS-like symptoms in mice.
source: Inspired by the finding that over-expression of mutant hSOD1 induces ALS-like symptoms in mouse (Gurney et al., 1994; Wong et al., 1995), we generated mouse ESC lines expressing high levels of wild type (WT) hSOD1, and hSOD1 with A4V or G93A mutations, both of which are genetic causes of familial ALS (Rosen, 1993; Gurney et al., 1994; Kiskinis et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Gurney et al., 1994 and Wong et al., 1995.

claim: hSOD1 A4V and G93A mutations are genetic causes of familial ALS.
source: Inspired by the finding that over-expression of mutant hSOD1 induces ALS-like symptoms in mouse (Gurney et al., 1994; Wong et al., 1995), we generated mouse ESC lines expressing high levels of wild type (WT) hSOD1, and hSOD1 with A4V or G93A mutations, both of which are genetic causes of familial ALS (Rosen, 1993; Gurney et al., 1994; Kiskinis et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Rosen, 1993; Gurney et al., 1994; Kiskinis et al., 2014.

claim: p62 serves as a selective autophagy receptor for protein aggregates.
source: p62 also serves as a selective autophagy receptor for protein aggregates (Dikic, 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Dikic, 2017.

claim: The inability to prevent the accumulation of insoluble protein aggregates could contribute to SpMN sensitivity to ALS.
source: Thus, the inability to prevent the accumulation of insoluble protein aggregates could contribute to SpMN sensitivity to ALS.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the observation that protein inclusions are a hallmark of ALS and that SpMNs accumulate more aggregates than CrMNs.

claim: ALS-sensitive SpMNs are under proteostatic stress during ALS progression.
source: Taken together, this evidence suggests that ALS-sensitive SpMNs are under proteostatic stress during ALS progression (Atkin et al., 2008; Matus et al., 2013; Hetz and Mollereau, 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Atkin et al., 2008; Matus et al., 2013; Hetz and Mollereau, 2014.

claim: ESC-derived iCrMNs and iSpMNs resemble the survival difference between ALS-resistant CrMNs and ALS-sensitive SpMNs.
source: Thus, ESC-derived iCrMNs and iSpMNs resemble the survival difference between ALS-resistant CrMNs and ALS-sensitive SpMNs.
evidence: This claim is supported by survival assay data comparing ESC-derived and primary motor neurons shown in Figures 1D and 1G.

claim: ESC-derived iCrMNs and iSpMNs resemble molecular features of the ALS-resistant O/TrMNs and ALS-sensitive SpMNs, respectively.
source: Thus, the comparative transcriptome analysis further supports the notion that ESC-derived iCrMNs and iSpMNs resemble molecular features of the ALS-resistant O/TrMNs and ALS-sensitive SpMNs, respectively.
evidence: This claim is supported by single-cell RNA sequencing analysis shown in Figure 1H-I and Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: ESC-derived motor neurons have the potential to represent intrinsic properties of their counterparts in vivo.
source: iCrMNs and iSpMNs recapitulated the differential survival of primary motor neurons under the same culture conditions, suggesting that ESC-derived motor neurons have the potential to represent intrinsic properties of their counterparts in vivo.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the observation that ESC-derived neurons showed similar survival patterns to primary neurons.

claim: CrMN resistance to ALS neurodegeneration is not limited to SOD1-linked ALS.
source: CrMN resistance to ALS neurodegeneration is not limited to SOD1-linked ALS.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the observation that non-transgenic iCrMNs are more resistant to general proteostatic stress, suggesting a mechanism independent of specific ALS mutations.

claim: iCrMNs rely more on the proteasome pathway to prevent the accumulation of p62-containing insoluble aggregates than iSpMNs.
source: These data suggest that CrMNs use the proteasome pathway more efficiently than SpMNs to prevent the accumulation of p62-containing insoluble aggregates.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the observation that MG-132 treatment caused greater accumulation of p62 aggregates in iCrMNs than iSpMNs.
